design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA cited as the reporting guideline; no protocol or registration mentioned) of studies in which a measure taken before a classic psychedelic (psilocybin, LSD, ayahuasca or DMT, mescaline) was reported to predict an acute drug effect. One database (PubMed): 42 searches crossing six drug terms with seven predictor terms, filtered to English, human studies and 1994 onward; the search date is not reported (manuscript received 8 January 2021). Two authors screened 1635 records; 10 articles met the criteria and 4 more were added from outside sources (for example reference lists or papers published after the search), 14 in all. The synthesis is narrative, organised by drug and then by 'states' and 'traits' (Tables 1 and 2): no pooled estimates, no tabulated effect sizes, no formal risk-of-bias assessment. The inclusion rule required that a pre-drug measure was predictive of an acute effect, so only reported associations were tabulated, never predictors tested and found null.
can_establish: Which pre-drug states, traits and biological measures had been reported, in 14 studies published before early 2021, as associated with acute effects of classic psychedelics, in which direction, and in what kinds of designs and samples: a map of reported associations and a pointer to the primary studies.
cannot_establish: How strong or consistent any predictor is (no effect sizes were pooled, and studies reporting no association were excluded by the inclusion rule); whether any predictor causes a better or more difficult experience; how the experience was measured in each study (the review names no instruments); or that the state predictors highlighted in the abstract were measured before the drug, since four of the 14 studies, including both sources of those states, are marked retrospective, with the 'baseline' states reported after the experience.

sample.recruitment: Literature search of PubMed only: two authors independently ran 42 searches crossing six drug terms (ayahuasca, LSD, lysergic acid diethylamide, mescaline, psilocybin, n,n-dimethyltryptamine) with seven predictor terms (predict, correlate, associate, pre-drug, individual difference, baseline, risk factor), filtered to English, human and 1994 to present (Methods › Search Strategy, 1st paragraph). Primary-study samples (Table 1): healthy volunteers in laboratory studies (Lebedev 2015, Lewis 2020, Carhart-Harris 2015, Terhune 2016, Stenbaek 2020, Studerus 2012); expert Buddhist meditators on a retreat (Smigielski 2019); long-term AIDS survivors in open-label group therapy (Stauffer 2020); people experienced with ayahuasca (Bouso 2013); and unselected people (Table 1's term): an analysis of reports posted on Erowid (Bienemann 2020), retrospective surveys of people who had used psilocybin (Carbonaro 2016; Russ 2019a and 2019b; how they were recruited is not stated in the review) and a prospective survey of people planning to take a psychedelic (Haijen 2018).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed articles in which classic psychedelic drugs were used and a pre-drug measure predicted an acute effect. Excluded: book chapters, case reports and reviews. Discrepancies were resolved by evaluating the study together with several team members (Methods › Selection Criteria, 1st paragraph). The 1994 limit is justified as the start of modern US administration studies; the English-language limit is not justified.
sample.demographics: Sample sizes 10 to 1993 (the review's printed mean and SD cannot be reproduced; see reporting issues); median publication year 2018. Examples from the text: 1993 respondents to an online survey of challenging experiences with psilocybin mushrooms (78% men, 89% white); 10 healthy volunteers given LSD intravenously in one laboratory (one woman; on average 65 previous LSD experiences), the same 10 analysed in two articles; 15 volunteers (two women) and 55 volunteers (22 women) in psilocybin imaging studies; 38 expert meditators (39 in Table 1); 18 long-term AIDS survivors, almost all older men, in open-label group therapy; 261 volunteers (100 women) from 23 pooled laboratory studies (Results › Drugs, all subsections).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Attrition within primary studies is mentioned only for Haijen et al. (2018).
sample.selection_effects: One database, English only, no grey literature, trial registries or systematic citation searching; the 4 extra articles were added ad hoc. The inclusion rule admitted only studies reporting a predictive association, so null findings were excluded by design (the authors name the file-drawer problem). Nine of the 14 articles come from two research groups: six include R.L. Carhart-Harris as an author (Carhart-Harris 2015, Terhune 2016, Lebedev 2015, both Russ 2019 articles, Haijen 2018) and three F.X. Vollenweider (Studerus 2012, Lewis 2020, Smigielski 2019) (editors' check of the reference list). The two LSD articles share one sample of 10.

exposure.measurement: Whatever each primary study used; the review does not name the instruments. Predictors are classed in Table 1 as states (S) or traits (T); age is classed as a state. Four studies are marked retrospective (Table 1, footnote a): Bienemann 2020 (an analysis of negative psilocybin reports posted to Erowid), Carbonaro 2016 (a survey of people who had used psilocybin about their most challenging experience) and Russ 2019a and 2019b (samples Table 1 calls unselected). The review does not say how the Carbonaro or Russ respondents were recruited; its Limitations paragraph mentions online crowd-sourcing only as a general feature of retrospective designs. In the two Russ studies the 'baseline' states (surrender, apprehension, preoccupation, confusion, deservingness, spiritual motivation) were therefore reported after the experience.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as tabulated in Table 1: psilocybin by mouth at fixed or weight-adjusted amounts in laboratory and clinical studies, or 'varied' (unknown) in the naturalistic and online studies; LSD 40-80 µg intravenously in one laboratory sample; psilocybin 2 mg intravenously in one study; ayahuasca 100 mL by mouth in one study. Dose was not used as a moderator in the synthesis.
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed. Two tabulated predictors are other drug histories (cannabis and alcohol consumption, from Studerus 2012); drugs taken alongside the psychedelic in the naturalistic studies are not discussed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable at review level; not reported for the primary studies.

comparison.controls: Variation in each predictor within each study's drug condition. Six of 14 studies had a control condition (placebo or a drug-naive group), which the review uses as a mark of quality, but the predictor analyses themselves are between-person associations under the drug.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not addressed. Dose, setting, drug identity and purity varied, uncontrolled, within the naturalistic and online studies; the review names these as limitations study by study but does not treat them as possible confounders of the tabulated associations.

outcomes.instruments: Not named. Outcomes are listed as constructs in Table 1, for example mystical experience, challenging experience, dread, ego dissolution, oceanic boundlessness, visionary restructuralization, 'bad trip', acute impairment of executive function, suggestibility, stimulus-colour consistency and intensity of the emotional experience. Some are not acute effects: well-being after use (Haijen 2018, Table 1) and spiritual change and long-term positive change (Russ 2019b; Table 2 and Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 6th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed; the review does not say which questionnaires were used, when they were rated or by whom.
outcomes.operationalization: A study entered if a pre-drug measure was reported as related to an acute effect. Table 1 gives only the sign of each association; the text quotes correlations for some studies (see effect sizes). 'Positive' and 'adverse' reactions are the primary studies' constructs, never defined by the review.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None at review level, where no tests were run; 76 is the editors' count of predictor-outcome associations tabulated in Table 1, each reported as significant by its primary study. The primary studies' own multiplicity handling is not reported; 19 of the 76 come from one study (Studerus 2012), which tested many predictors against many outcomes, so chance findings are likely among them.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Two authors screened records; how data were extracted, and by whom, is not described.

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled or tabulated. Correlations and other effect sizes quoted in the text: Russ 2019b (n = 143) surrender r = 0.72 and absorption r = 0.61 with mystical-type experience, preoccupation r = 0.64 and confusion r = 0.58 with dread, age r = -0.23 with dread; Stauffer 2020 (n = 18, open label) attachment anxiety r = 0.53 with mystical-type experience and attachment avoidance r = 0.62 with challenging experience; Carbonaro 2016 (n = 1993) age r = -0.06 and history of hallucinogen use r = -0.05 with difficulty of the experience; Carhart-Harris 2015 (n = 10) conscientiousness r = 0.89 with change in suggestibility and imagery ability r = 0.72 with change in imagery; Terhune 2016 (same 10 people) absorption r = -0.67 with stimulus-colour consistency; Bouso 2013 (n = 24) lifetime ayahuasca use r = -0.62 with executive impairment; Bienemann 2020 (n = 346) sex and 'bad trip' reports V = 0.20, called small. Editors' calculation: correlations of -0.05 and -0.06 correspond to under 0.4% of shared variance.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; PRISMA is cited (Methods › Search Strategy, 1st paragraph). The supporting information, a spreadsheet of the same results organised by outcome, is a download and was not opened.
analysis.selective_reporting: Built into the design: the inclusion rule admits only predictors reported as predictive, so the review cannot show predictors that were tested and not found (the authors acknowledge the file-drawer problem in Limitations). The abstract and Conclusion present absorption as a predictor of positive and mystical-type experiences and omit that, in the one prospective naturalistic study, absorption was also associated with challenging experiences (Table 1 and Table 2 show it; in Haijen 2018's Table 7 the coefficients were 0.215 for challenging and 0.347 for mystical-type experience).
analysis.power: Not addressed. Eight of the 14 samples have 55 or fewer participants (editors' count from Table 1: 10, 10, 15, 16, 18, 24, 39 and 55).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 14 mostly small or retrospective studies, the trait absorption was reported as positively associated with mystical-type or oceanic experiences in four (Studerus 2012, both Russ 2019 articles, Haijen 2018), but in the only prospective naturalistic study (Haijen 2018) absorption was also positively associated with challenging experiences and visual effects. The state predictors in the abstract (surrender, apprehension, preoccupation, confusion) come from two retrospective online studies by the same team. A positive 'set' the day before (fewer challenging experiences), clear intentions (more mystical-type experience) and recreational intentions (fewer challenging experiences) come from one prospective study. Acceptance rests on one study of 38 or 39 expert meditators, and each biological predictor on a single study of 15, 16 or 55 people. In the largest study, age and history of hallucinogen use correlated with difficulty at r = -0.06 and -0.05.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says people high in absorption, openness and acceptance and in a state of surrender were more likely to have positive and mystical-type experiences, and the Conclusion that such people “may represent ideal candidates for psychedelic therapy”. Gaps: (1) the state predictors were reported after the experience in their only two sources, yet are presented as baseline predictors; (2) absorption's association with challenging experiences in the one prospective study is left out of the abstract and Conclusion; (3) the 'ideal candidates' statement rests on healthy volunteers and people using psychedelics on their own, not on therapy outcomes in patients; (4) the abstract infers that people become slightly less sensitive after repeated use, and the Discussion that overuse may blunt benefits, from between-person correlations that equally fit selection (people who had difficult experiences may stop using); (5) the abstract and Conclusion call the anterior cingulate predictor a volume, while the cited study measured cortical thickness; (6) the Future Directions section speculates about changing baseline traits before treatment, which no included study tested. The Limitations paragraph is frank about small, open-label and self-selected samples, but those limits do not reach the abstract.

timeline.event: Studerus et al. pooled 23 psilocybin laboratory studies (261 volunteers) to find predictors of response; the review includes it and calls it an earlier overview that was not systematic and covered one laboratory and one drug.
Haijen et al. prospective online study of people planning to take a psychedelic; the review's only prospective naturalistic source of set and intention predictors.
Russ et al., two retrospective online studies (183 and 143 people), one titled a replication and extension of the Studerus 2012 model; the sole sources of the review's state predictors.
Studerus et al. applied the pooled-laboratory predictor approach to MDMA (194 volunteers).
Vizeli et al. applied it to LSD (213 volunteers) and cite this review.

replication.where_it_stands: The first systematic review of pre-drug predictors of acute psychedelic effects, by its authors' account, mapping a small and early literature. Because it admits only positive findings, does not appraise or weight studies by design and contains sign errors in its tables, claims should cite the primary studies (Haijen 2018 for set and intentions measured before use; the Basel pooled laboratory analyses for mood and personality measured before dosing) and use this review as a pointer, not as evidence that a predictor is consistent or strong.

funding.funder: No funding for the review is stated. Effort for Dr. Davis was provided by Tim Ferriss, Matt Mullenweg, Craig Nerenberg, Blake Mycoskie and the Steven and Alexandra Cohen Foundation; the statement says the funders had no role in study design, data analysis, the decision to publish or preparation of the manuscript.
funding.declared_conflicts: Dr. Davis is a board member of Source Research Foundation; the statement says this organization was not involved in the design or execution of the study or in the interpretation or communication of findings.
funding.affiliations_note: Four authors in the Department of Psychology, Central Michigan University; A.K. Davis at the College of Social Work, The Ohio State University, and the Center for Psychedelic and Consciousness Research, Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. No review author is an author of an included study (editors' check of the reference list).

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered individual-participant meta-analysis of prospective studies, in laboratories, clinics and naturalistic settings, in which states, traits and intentions are measured before the drug with validated instruments, the experience is rated with the same questionnaires (for example MEQ30, CEQ, 5D-ASC) at a fixed time, every predictor tested is reported whether or not it was significant, and models allow for dose, drug, setting and prior experience.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Components stated broadly: humans given classic psychedelics, any pre-drug measure, any acute effect; a comparator does not apply to a question about predictors. The outcome is defined only as 'an acute effect', and non-acute outcomes were nevertheless included.

Chapters, case reports and reviews were excluded; no reason is given for admitting every other design, including analyses of posted online reports and retrospective surveys, alongside placebo-controlled studies.

One database (PubMed) with stated keywords; English only without justification; no grey literature, registries, systematic reference-list searching or expert contact; search date not reported; 4 of 14 articles added ad hoc. Partial yes requires at least two databases.
Two authors independently searched and assessed the 1635 records; discrepancies were resolved with several team members (Methods › Selection Criteria; Results › Study Selection, 1st paragraph).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: No list of excluded full texts or reasons; the flow diagram (Figure 1) is an image and could not be viewed in this reading.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives population, drug, dose and route, sample size, control condition, predictor, outcome and direction, with retrospective designs flagged; settings, instruments, timing of measurement and effect sizes are not given.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No tool or stated method. The prose names limitations study by study (sample size, open label, retrospective design, uncontrolled dose and setting, self-selection), unevenly, and calls some studies methodologically rigorous without stating criteria. A close call against partial yes, which would need confounding and selection bias assessed across the studies.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Limitations paragraph discusses designs in general, but the abstract and Conclusion present predictors from retrospective online studies (the state predictors) and from single small studies (acceptance, the brain measures) as if equivalent to prospectively measured ones.

The conflicting sex findings are discussed with alternative explanations, but not why absorption relates to both mystical and challenging experiences, nor differences between laboratory and naturalistic designs, outcomes or drugs.
No quantitative synthesis. The file-drawer problem is named in Limitations, and the inclusion rule itself (only predictive associations) selects on positive results.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Support for one author and his board membership are declared.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Critical items 2, 4, 7, 9 and 13 are not met (no protocol, a one-database English-only search, no list of excluded studies, no risk-of-bias assessment, and conclusions that do not account for study design), so confidence is critically low by the AMSTAR 2 rule. Beyond the AMSTAR items, the inclusion rule admits only positive associations, so the review cannot speak to consistency, and its tables contain sign errors and an impossible summary statistic (reporting issues). The review may be cited as a map of predictors reported up to early 2021 and as a pointer to primary studies; it should not be cited as evidence that any predictor is consistent or strong, for the claim that preparation-related states predict experiences (their sources are retrospective), or for the 'ideal candidates for therapy' conclusion.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: PubMed only, 42 searches (six drug terms by seven predictor terms), English, human, 1994 to present, search date not reported; two authors assessed 1635 records; 10 articles met the criteria and 4 were added from outside sources, 14 in all.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Search Strategy, 1st paragraph; Methods › Selection Criteria, 1st paragraph; Results › Study Selection, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Included studies: 10 on psilocybin, 2 on LSD (both from the same 10 participants), 1 on ayahuasca, 1 on psychedelics in general; sample sizes 10 to 1993; 6 of 14 with a control condition; 4 with a retrospective design; median publication year 2018.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study Selection, 2nd paragraph; Table 1 and footnote a; Results › Drugs › LSD, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Absorption was tabulated with more mystical-type experience, ego dissolution, oceanic boundlessness and visionary restructuralization and less dread, and also with more challenging experience and visual effects (Haijen 2018) and less stimulus-colour consistency (Terhune 2016); sources Studerus 2012, Russ 2019a and 2019b, Terhune 2016 and Haijen 2018. In Russ 2019b (n = 143, retrospective) absorption correlated r = 0.61 with mystical-type experience.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (absorption row); Table 1 (Haijen rows); Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 6th paragraph; Discussion › Traits, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: All state predictors named in the abstract (surrender, apprehension, preoccupation, confusion), with deservingness and spiritual motivation, come from Russ 2019a (n = 183) and Russ 2019b (n = 143), both marked retrospective. In Russ 2019b surrender correlated r = 0.72 with mystical-type experience, and preoccupation r = 0.64 and confusion r = 0.58 with dread.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (Russ rows, footnote a); Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Discussion › States, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: From the one prospective naturalistic study (Haijen 2018; 212 to 654 participants across time points): a positive 'set' just before use went with fewer challenging experiences, clear intentions with more mystical-type experience and visual effects, and recreational intentions with fewer challenging experiences; the review notes attrition and varied substances, doses and settings as limits.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drugs › Psychedelics Not Otherwise Specified, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (set, clear intention and recreational intention rows); Discussion › States, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Table 1 prints the sign for set and challenging experience as positive, contradicting Table 2 and the text (reporting issues); the text also attributes to set associations that Haijen 2018 reports only for clear intentions.

key_findings.finding: Openness was tabulated with fewer adverse experiences (Russ 2019a) and more oceanic boundlessness and mystical experience (Smigielski 2019); acceptance with mystical experience in Smigielski 2019 only, a placebo-controlled study of expert Buddhist meditators on a retreat (38 in the text, 39 in Table 1; 15 women).
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (openness and acceptance rows); Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 7th paragraph; Discussion › Traits, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sex: only Bienemann 2020, an analysis of 346 negative psilocybin reports posted to Erowid, found 'bad trips' more often reported by women (V = 0.20, called small); three studies with adverse-reaction measures found no sex difference, and the review judges sex not a robust predictor.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 4th paragraph; Discussion › Traits, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Age and previous use: in Carbonaro 2016 (n = 1993; 78% men, 89% white), age r = -0.06 and history of hallucinogen use r = -0.05 with difficulty of the experience; in Studerus 2012 age went with less impaired control and cognition and previous psychedelic use with less disembodiment and visionary restructuralization; in Bouso 2013 (n = 24) lifetime ayahuasca use correlated r = -0.62 with executive impairment under ayahuasca. The review infers that older and more experienced people have generally less intense effects.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 8th and 10th paragraphs; Results › Drugs › Ayahuasca, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Traits, 4th paragraph; Discussion › States, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Biological predictors, each from one study: lower serotonin 2A receptor binding with longer peak effects, faster comedown and higher mystical-type ratings (Stenbaek 2020, n = 16, no control); lower executive-network node diversity with more ego dissolution (Lebedev 2015, n = 15, two women, placebo-controlled); right rostral anterior cingulate thickness with spiritual experience and insightfulness (Lewis 2020, n = 55).

Authors' stated limitations: many studies open label, small or homogeneous; self-selection in retrospective online designs; most relationships unreplicated; possible unpublished null results (file drawer).

reporting_issues.issue: The review gives the sample sizes as ranging from 10 to 1993 with a mean of 108.75 and SD of 91.95. From Table 1 the mean is 237.5 (SD 517) taking Haijen 2018 as 212, or 269.1 (SD 529) taking it as 654, and with one value of 1993 among 14 studies and a mean of 108.75 the SD could not be below about 523 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed summary cannot be correct for the studies in Table 1; quote sample sizes from the table, not from the summary.

reporting_issues.issue: Signs disagree between tables: for Haijen 2018, set and challenging experience is positive in Table 1 but negative in Table 2 and in the text; for Lebedev 2015, executive-network node diversity and ego dissolution is negative in Table 1 and in the text but positive in Table 2.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1; Table 2; Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Table 2, the summary most readers will use, carries a reversed sign for node diversity, and Table 1 a reversed sign for set; use the text and the primary studies.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives openness and well-being in Haijen 2018 as negative, whereas Haijen 2018 (read in this session; Table 6) reports openness positively associated with well-being at baseline (B = 1.500, p = 0.002) and two weeks after (B = 1.273, p = 0.030). Table 1 also leaves the direction blank for history of psychedelic use and well-being, which Table 2 gives as negative.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's openness entry for Haijen is reversed; well-being after use is also outside the review's own scope of acute effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The text summarises Haijen 2018 as finding that clear intentions and a positive set were both conducive to mystical-type experiences and visual effects and decreased challenging experiences; in Haijen's Table 7, set was associated only with lower challenging-experience scores (beta -0.324; with mystical-type experience 0.014, p = 0.835) and clear intentions only with mystical-type experience and visual effects (with challenging experience -0.134, p = 0.088).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Drugs › Psychedelics Not Otherwise Specified, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite Haijen 2018 directly for which state predicted which outcome.

reporting_issues.issue: The anterior cingulate predictor is called 'rACC volume' in the abstract, Tables 1 and 2, Discussion and Conclusion, but 'thickness' in Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 3rd paragraph, and in the cited study's title; the Discussion (Traits, 1st paragraph) cites it as reference 54 (Haijen) instead of 45 (Lewis).
reporting_issues.consequence: The biomarker should be described as cortical thickness, from Lewis et al. (2020).

reporting_issues.issue: Lewis 2020 is called a placebo-controlled study in the text, but Table 1 marks it as having no control condition; Smigielski 2019 has 39 participants in Table 1 and 38 in the text.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 3rd and 7th paragraphs; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The count of 6 controlled studies may be 7; check the primary studies before describing their designs.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives the psilocybin doses in Studerus 2012 as 115-315 mg/kg, a unit implausible for humans and unlike the µg/kg used for Smigielski 2019 in the same table; µg/kg is probably meant (not checked against Studerus 2012, which was not read).
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not take doses from this table.

reporting_issues.issue: The paragraph on Stenbaek 2020 reports that lower serotonin 2A binding went with higher mystical-type ratings, then gives an explanation in which greater receptor availability leads to more intense effects, the opposite direction, without comment.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the binding finding should be taken from the primary study.

reporting_issues.issue: Smaller mismatches between Table 1, Table 2 and the text: alcohol consumption goes with complex imagery in Table 1 but visual effects in Table 2; preoccupation and adverse experience (Russ 2019a) is in Table 1 but not Table 2; spiritual change appears only in Table 2; age is classed as a state; a sentence on Russ 2019b cites reference 44 (Lebedev) where 46 (Russ 2019a) is meant; and Table 2's openness row cites reference 54 (Haijen 2018) with 46 and 48, although none of the outcomes listed there (adverse experience, oceanic boundlessness, mystical experience) comes from Haijen 2018, whose openness entry in Table 1 concerns well-being.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Tables 1 and 2; Results › Drugs › Psilocybin, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The tables cannot be used interchangeably; check each entry against its primary study.
